learning_objective: 🎯 Master the art of 'anti-derivatives' to glue tiny pieces back together, allowing you to find total accumulated values and the area under any curve!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Integration is exactly the opposite of differentiation. If differentiating tells you the speed from the distance, integrating tells you the total distance traveled if you only know the speed!
When you integrate a general function, you must always add '+ C' (the constant of integration) because there are infinite parallel curves that have the exact same slope.

When an integral looks too complicated, you can simplify it by replacing a messy part of it with the letter 't'. The trick is finding a part whose derivative is also sitting right there in the equation.

This is the product rule for integration. When two different types of functions are multiplied (like x * sin(x)), you use a formula to split them up. The ILATE rule helps you choose which function is 'first'.
These have an upper and lower limit. You evaluate the integral and plug the limits in (Upper - Lower). The answer is an exact number, representing the exact area under the curve.

fun_activity.title: 🎨 Coloring Under the Curve
fun_activity.instructions: Draw a parabola $y = x^2$ on graph paper. Color the area bounded between the curve, the x-axis, and the lines $x=0$ and $x=2$. Definite integration is the mathematical tool that perfectly calculates how much colored area you just made!

exam_tips: 📌 NEVER forget to write '+ C' at the end of an Indefinite Integral. Examiners will aggressively deduct marks for this.
📌 Use the ILATE rule (Inverse, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential) to correctly select the 'First Function' when doing Integration by Parts.
📌 For Definite Integrals, memorize the standard properties (like $\int_0^a f(x)dx = \int_0^a f(a-x)dx$). They are the secret shortcut to solving 4-mark questions in seconds.
quick_recap: ⭐ Integration puts the derivative back to its original function.
⭐ Substitution is your first line of defense for tricky integrals.
⭐ Definite integrals calculate exact numerical areas, so they don't need a '+ C'.
